system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 8 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2180-01-31 19:03:00 to 2180-02-08 14:36:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 55-year-old woman was admitted for recurrent nausea and vomiting five days after laparoscopic repair of a colonic mesenteric defect. Initial evaluation, including CT imaging, ruled out postoperative complications or bowel obstruction. Symptoms were attributed to a flare of chronic gastroparesis. She was managed with NG tube placement, IV fluids, and antiemetics, showing improvement within 24 hours. The NG tube was removed on hospital day two, and her diet was advanced successfully. Her gastroenterologist recommended continued dromperidone and a low-fat, small-meal diet. She was discharged home on day three with stable vital signs, no nausea, and a plan to follow up with her primary care provider and gastroenterologist. No medication changes were made except for reducing omeprazole from 40 mg to 20 mg daily.

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  Woman with nausea, vomiting, recent hernia repair.  Evaluate for
obstruction.

COMPARISON:  Abdominal radiograph from ___.

TWO VIEWS OF THE ABDOMEN:  A lucency in the lower abdomen is noted which may
represent a focally dilated, relatively featureless loop of bowel or prominent
adjacent loops.  Air is seen in the rectum.  Right upper quadrant and left
upper quadrant clips are changed from the CT from ___.  Mild
dextroscoliosis is unchanged as well.

IMPRESSION:

Lucency in the lower abdomen may represent a focal dilated featureless loop of
bowel or prominent adjacent loops, and may represent ileus versus
partial/early obstruction.  Findings could be further evaluated on CT as
clinically warranted.

INDICATION:  ___ female with vomiting.  Evaluate for pneumonia.

COMPARISON:  ___.

PA AND LATERAL CHEST RADIOGRAPHS:  A nasogastric tube has been removed. 
Post-surgical changes in the left axilla and left upper quadrant are again
noted.  The lungs remain free of focal consolidation and there is no effusion
or pneumothorax.  The hilar and cardiomediastinal contours are stable.  The
descending aorta is again unfolded.  Pulmonary vasculature is normal in
caliber and distribution.  There is no pulmonary edema.  The bones extensive
thoracic spondylosis with suggesting of some end plate deformity in the mid
thoracic region, though not well evaluated on this study.

IMPRESSION:  
1.  No acute cardiopulmonary process, including no evidence of pneumonia.
2.  Degenerative change in the spine, with suggestion of end-plate deformity
of a mid-thoracic vertebral body, poorly evaluated on this study.  If there is
concern for bony injury, dedicated T-spine radiographs may be helpful.

INDICATION:  Mid thoracic pain.

COMPARISON:  CT of the abdomen and pelvis from ___.

TWO VIEWS OF THE THORAX:

There is a new compression fracture of two mid thoracic vertebral bodies. Also
noted are partially imaged clips in the left axilla.  The visible lungs are
clear.  The cardiomediastinal silhouette and hilar contours are normal.

IMPRESSION:

New compression fracture of two mid thoracic vertebral bodies.

REASON FOR EXAM:  Chronic nausea and vomiting, elevated total bilirubin and
LDH and leukocytosis.  Clinical concern for biliary ductal dilatation.

COMPARISON:  CT of the abdomen and pelvis from ___.

RIGHT UPPER QUADRANT ULTRASOUND:  Liver is echogenic.  There is no focal liver
lesion.  There is no intrahepatic biliary ductal dilatation.  The common bile
duct measures up to 7 mm. Portal vein is patent. The pancreatic duct measures
up to 3 mm, which is upper limit of normal.  There is a 1.6-cm right renal
cyst within the interpolar region.  Pancreatic head is grossly unremarkable. 
The remainder of the pancreas is obscured by overlying bowel gas.  

IMPRESSION:
1. Common bile duct measures up to 7 mm, which is upper limit of normal and
likely within normal limits for post-cholecystectomy state. No intrahepatic
biliary ductal dilatation.   Clinical correlation is recommended.

2. Echogenic liver compatible with fatty infiltration or hepatic
cirrhosis/fibrosis.

3. 1.6-cm right renal cyst.

PORTABLE ABDOMEN OF ___

COMPARISON:  Radiograph of two days earlier.

INDICATION:  Feeding tube placement.

FINDINGS:  Feeding tube terminates in the proximal stomach.  A non-obstructive
bowel gas pattern is visualized.

HISTORY:  ___ woman with gastroparesis, needing Dobbhoff tube post-
pyloric.

NASOINTESTINAL TUBE PLACEMENT

FINDINGS:  The patient's right nare was anesthetized with 1% viscous
lidocaine.  A feeding catheter was advanced through the right naris into the
stomach with the tip in a post-pyloric position, which was confirmed after
injection of 10 cc of Conray.  The tube was flushed with water and secured to
the patient's nose.

IMPRESSION:  Successful post-pyloric nasointestinal tube placement.

procedures.long_title: Enteral infusion of concentrated nutritional substances

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You came in with nausea and vomiting again—can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I woke up this morning feeling nauseous and vomited just spit—no food, nothing. I haven’t eaten anything today. It’s been like this for a few days now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any pain in your belly when you vomit?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just a general ache, nothing sharp. No diarrhea or blood in stool.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And you mentioned back pain too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s usually there, but today it’s worse—especially when I move. It’s a nagging pain, maybe a 6 out of 10.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No numbness, tingling, or trouble with bladder or bowels?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, none of that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get some labs and imaging. Your white blood cell count is high—17.4—so we’re checking for infection, but your chest X-ray looks clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not usually. We’ll keep an eye on it. We also did a spine X-ray because of your back pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I’ve had back issues before, but it’s never this bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got the T-spine film back. There’s a new compression fracture in two of your mid-back bones. That’s likely why the pain is worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A fracture? But I didn’t fall or anything!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With chronic conditions like yours and possible osteoporosis, bones can weaken. Sometimes even normal movement can cause a fracture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s scary. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not an emergency, but it needs attention. We’ll manage the pain and make sure you follow up with your primary doctor about bone health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures came back—no infection. The high white count is likely from stress or inflammation, not an active infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not needed. We’re focusing on your gastroparesis and nutrition. You’ve lost 50 pounds in a year—that’s a big concern.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just can’t keep food down. I’ve tried everything—meds, Botox, small meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re talking with your gastroenterologist. They want a J-tube, but surgery wants to try a temporary feeding tube first—goes past the stomach into the small intestine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A tube in my nose again? I hate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s temporary. Helps us see if feeding past the stomach works before doing surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, if it helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The Dobhoff tube is in—placed past your stomach. We’ll start slow feeding today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Already? How will I feel?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most people don’t feel it much. We’ll watch for nausea. If you tolerate it, this could be a step toward better nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—you’ve had the feeding tube for two days, no nausea or vomiting. Your labs are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? I didn’t even notice it after the first day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. It means your body can handle nutrition past the stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I pulled the tube out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did? Are you feeling okay? Any nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel fine. I just want to go home. I’m tired of being here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But we need to plan next steps. The tube worked well—your team may still recommend a permanent J-tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll think about it. Can I go home now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll work on discharge. But please follow up with your GI and surgeon to discuss options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your potassium was low when you came in—2.6. That can make you weak and affect your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it better now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s 4.1 now. We’ll send you home with potassium pills—one daily, especially if you vomit again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure has been high—up to 170/99. We started you on metoprolol. Stress and pain can raise it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been anxious. Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not acutely, but long-term it’s important to control. Keep taking the medication and monitor at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need it forever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Your PCP can reassess once things settle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. Your nausea is controlled, labs are stable, and you’re walking fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about the back pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve been using ketorolac and Valium as needed. You’ll go home with naproxen—a similar medicine—for one week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the fracture?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Follow up with your primary doctor about osteoporosis. They may start treatment to strengthen your bones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re being discharged home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What meds am I taking now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same ones: citalopram, levothyroxine, omeprazole. New ones: Zofran and Compazine for nausea if it returns, potassium daily, and naproxen for back pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the feeding tube decision?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still important to discuss with GI and surgery. The temporary tube worked, so a permanent one might help long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make the appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, get your labs done next week—Chem 10—and fax the results to your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if nausea returns or pain worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon, I hope not!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hopefully not! But we’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I avoid lifting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially with the spine fracture. No heavy lifting for several weeks. Use caution with movement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And keep using the lidocaine patch for back pain if it helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright, the discharge papers are ready. You’re free to go when you’re set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Stay hydrated, eat small meals, and follow up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Bye!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye!

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, one last question—can I drive?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you’re not on strong pain meds and feel alert, yes. But listen to your body.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m off the IV meds, so I think I’m okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Then yes, you can drive. Just take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye!

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye!

summary.summary_paragraph: A 55-year-old woman was admitted for recurrent nausea and vomiting, with a history of chronic gastroparesis, recent paraduodenal hernia repair, and multiple prior hospitalizations for similar symptoms. She presented with inability to tolerate oral intake, generalized abdominal pain with vomiting, and new-onset worsening back pain. Initial evaluation revealed leukocytosis, hypokalemia, and a non-obstructive bowel pattern. Imaging identified a new compression fracture in two mid-thoracic vertebrae. A post-pyloric Dobhoff tube was placed and enteral feeding initiated, which she tolerated well for two days before self-removing the tube and expressing readiness for discharge. Her nausea resolved, electrolytes normalized, and pain was controlled with medications. She was discharged home with improved symptoms, new prescriptions for antiemetics, potassium supplementation, and naproxen for back pain, and instructions to follow up with her gastroenterologist and primary care provider regarding long-term feeding options and osteoporosis management.
